rounds.what: One code commit and a forward merge since round 3. The round's correctness change — a confirming read the replacement's delete overtakes answering Uncertain — was driven by reproducing the defect it fixes; the SQL-backed session reader was driven against a real PostgreSQL 16 with one case the implementer's run did not cover; and the deleted-world sweep was re-derived with its own published commands and extended to the half those commands do not reach.

implementerProof.how: Round 4: I re-ran this round's correctness proof as a defect reproduction of my own (disabling the generation comparison rather than taking its negative control on trust), and re-ran the SQL reader's statements against a real PostgreSQL I started myself, extending them to `session_copy`'s prefix query, which its run did not cover. Its skills-guard proof I confirmed by reading the guard's own numbers at this head rather than re-running the suite. Its fingerprint proof I did not recompute: it reports the diff unchanged across a merge that touched one file of main's, and the code I tested is the code at this head. Rounds 1 to 3: each re-run independently as those rounds record, with every negative control performed by me.

proof.criterion: A confirming read the replacement's delete overtakes is Uncertain, not a final Gone that charges a death the daemon itself made.
proof.surface: The sandbox package's rig — the real `relaunch`, `evaluate` and `Probe` paths against a fake dynamic client — driven as a defect reproduction in an out-of-tree copy of the module.
proof.command: Disable the generation comparison in `evaluate` (`false && nowAt != heldAt`) and run the round's test; restore and run all five gap tests together
proof.observed: Without the guard: `TestAConfirmingReadTheReplacementsDeleteOvertakesIsUncertain` fails — `gone, Displaced false (no pod of sandbox legion-legion-legion-208 (operatingMode Suspended)); want Uncertain`. That is the death the daemon made, delivered as final. Restored, the five gap tests of rounds 3 and 4 pass together.
proof.negativeControl: My round-3 lock still fails under its own mutation (the kept name's uid comparison dropped) at this head, so the new generation guard did not subsume or swallow it; the two guards are independent.

proof.criterion: The e2e harness's SQL-backed session reader, the round's blocking fix, reads what the session database holds.
proof.surface: A real PostgreSQL 16 started as a workload in the cluster and reached by its Service name from this pod, carrying Oh My Pi's own two tables created with the statements `internal/ompsessions/ompsessions.go` declares, driven with the exact statements `session_text` and `session_copy` run, the path bound as a parameter as `:'path'` binds it.
proof.command: A Go program against that database: create the tables, seed one row with two parts inserted at offset 200 then 100 and two neighbouring keys, then run the reader's statement for the key, for an absent path and for an injected path, and the copy's prefix statement for the parent's stem
proof.observed: The row's content, then the part at offset 100, then the one at offset 200 — start_offset order and not insert order — 117 bytes byte-for-byte identical to what was seeded, with embedded escaped quotes, a tab and the trailing newline intact. An absent path answers no row at all, which is what makes the reader fail naming the path as the old `cat` of a missing file did. `x'; DROP TABLE omp_session_files; --` matched no row and left all three rows standing. And `session_copy`'s prefix query, which the implementer's run did not cover, takes the subagent's key alone under the parent's stem — not the parent's own key, not another session's.
proof.negativeControl: The absent path and the injected path are the controls: each is a read that must answer nothing, and the table's row count after the injected path is the proof the parameter was never spliced.
proof.doesNotSettle: A reader proven against a database is not a harness proven against a pod. Neither my run nor the implementer's touches `docker exec` into the run's database container, which is the devbox's path and exists nowhere else; `claim_session_file`'s read of the claims CLI; or any of the ten-plus call sites now routed through the reader. `psql`'s own `-A -t` formatting and `:'path'` quoting are covered by the implementer's Job and by nothing of mine. Stage 4b has run at no head.

Recovery vocabulary: every hit is a negative assertion — two `grep -c 'volume was lost'` counts compared for equality and the marker path used to assert absence. Stage 4a: clean, and by more than the published command — that command greps only `scripts/`, while Stage 4a's checks are the Go live tests, which I grepped too; every session mention there is a key passed as `ResumeSessionFile` or built for the absent-session refusal, and the only `cat` is `markerLines`, which reads the marker. The two documentation residues remain unfixed (see findingsNotFailures).

proof.criterion: The cutover's displacement window: a sibling role read while the issue has no Sandbox at all is the daemon's own end, not a death.

proof.observed: Both fail without it — `read while no Sandbox of the issue exists: gone, Displaced false; want Gone and Displaced` — including the window a failed Create holds open until the issue's next launch. Both pass restored.

proof.criterion: 1. The claim template's metadata, and the immutability the cutover rests on, on a real API server.
proof.surface: A real kube-apiserver v1.37 with the pinned Agent Sandbox CRD and the daemon's own goldens; re-run in round 3 with the controller goldens, which came back with no `initContainers` key at all.
proof.command: create the goldens; POST one with labels on the ephemeral claim template, with and without strict field validation; patch `spec.volumeClaimTemplates` onto a live Sandbox; then the cutover's patch-delete-create sequence
proof.observed: The rendered Sandbox is accepted unchanged. A labelled claim template is pruned — 201 with stored metadata `{}` and a `warning: 299` header, and refused outright under strict validation. `volumeClaimTemplates is immutable` on a live Sandbox. The suspension's merge patch returns 200 carrying the displaced-pod annotation in its own response, and the replacement carrying it is accepted.
proof.negativeControl: The strict-validation refusal is the control for the pruning, and the immutability refusal for the delete-and-create.

proof.criterion: 1. The disk is created with its pod and deleted with it, at today's size and storage.
proof.surface: A real Kubernetes cluster — the build namespace this worker pod may submit Jobs to — running a pod that declares the same ephemeral claim template the issue goldens show, with the namespace's claim counter as the observation. The cluster is this deployment's; the class is the build namespace's own scratch class, not the issue volumes' class. The issue pod's volume block is byte-identical from `b650d854` to this head.
proof.command: apply the Job; poll the claim counter through the pod's life; read the pod's own `spec.volumes[0]` and its log; delete the Job
proof.observed: The counter went 0 → 1 while the pod was still Pending; the disk came up holding `lost+found` alone and took a 16 MiB write; the counter stayed at 1 after the pod Completed, so the claim's life is the pod object's; and it was back to 0 between two polls about a second apart, which is an upper bound and not a timing.
proof.negativeControl: The same Job with one label on that claim template was refused by the namespace's admission policy naming the rule.

proof.criterion: 6. The upgrade half of the cutover: an issue_suspend row the running release queued must still run after the upgrade.
proof.surface: A real PostgreSQL 16 run as a workload in the cluster, carrying the daemon's own schema, driven by the daemon's own migration runner and enqueue path, with the payload bytes the previous release's struct produces.
proof.command: migrate; delete the schema_version row for 51; enqueue the two rows that release writes, one mid-retry; decode; migrate again; decode
proof.observed: At schema 50 the head binary refuses the releasing row — `json: unknown field "release"`. The upgrade applied exactly 1 migration. Both rows then decode, with attempts, next_at, last_error and created_at byte-identical, so a row mid-retry keeps its backoff.
proof.negativeControl: The keeping row, written without the key, decoded before the migration and was untouched by it.

proof.criterion: 5. No code is left that reuses, repairs or inspects a disk from an earlier pod, with the stale git-lock sweep kept for the retry on the same disk.
proof.surface: The tree, plus the one runtime surface where a provision can still meet a non-empty disk: the kubelet restarts a failed init container in the same pod.
proof.command: the deletion grep, then `provision` into a root it had already provisioned after planting this issue's own production failure signature
proof.observed: 17 hits, all history or negative assertions. With the planted bad ref, provision exits 1 in 0.98 s with `fatal: bad object refs/jj/keep/badref` — no repair, no hang, which is what leaves the pod replaceable.
proof.negativeControl: With four stale git locks planted instead, the same command removed each by name and exited 0.

findingsNotFailures.what: `scripts/e2e/README.md:965`'s `pod-baseline` row promises the stub agent's environment carries `OMP_SESSION_STORAGE=file`, while `live_operator_test.go:179-183` now requires `ompsessions.SQLStorage` — a flat contradiction in the proof's own published contract. The reviewer raised it and the setup-negative row with it; this round carried both rather than fixing them.
findingsNotFailures.evidence: Read at this head: the README row's text, and the `want` map in `live_operator_test.go` naming `ompsessions.StorageVariable: ompsessions.SQLStorage`.
findingsNotFailures.verdict: A finding to fix in this pull request, not a round failure, and consistent with my round-3 ruling on the cutover's selector sentence: no check is weakened and nothing an operator or an agent does goes wrong — what is wrong is the row a reader uses to learn what the check proves. Worth naming once more because it is the same class as round 2's three lifecycle rows, which were fixed rather than carried; carrying two of a class that was fixed twice is the inconsistency, not the rows themselves.

findingsNotFailures.what: The code commit of this round, `862a809d38df`, is authored by the **review** App (343353696+legion-reviewer) with the implement App as its committer and the implementer's session in its `Omp-Session` trailer.
findingsNotFailures.evidence: `jj log -r 862a809d38df -T 'author.email() ++ committer.email() ++ description'`: author `343353696+legion-reviewer[bot]`, committer `343353655+legion-implementer[bot]`, `Omp-Session: 01a17058-…`, the implementer's session.
findingsNotFailures.verdict: Not a failure and nothing to pin: no gate reads a code commit's author, and `handoff_complete` checks only the handoff commit's, which is the implement App's and correct. It is the shape `skill://legion-worker` warns about — a `split` or `describe` of the working-copy commit found at the turn's start, which keeps the previous role's author — and the previous role here was the reviewer, whose empty working copy the implementer inherited. Reported so the architect can have the habit corrected rather than the history rewritten; rewriting a pushed commit for attribution alone would cost more than it buys.

The thread replies named beside the path do survive, so nothing is lost; the citation would be better if it led with them. I followed the durable form for my own round: round 4's evidence is a pull request comment, linked from the body.

residualRisks: The generation counter this round adds is one counter for every Sandbox name, so a strand or unstrand for another issue while a confirming read is out costs this read an Uncertain and a tick's delay. The code says so; the cost is bounded and the alternative, a per-name counter deleted with its record, reads the same before a strand and after its unstrand.

A daemon that restarts inside the gap a migrating replacement opens has neither the Sandbox nor the kept name, and reads those roles' ends as deaths. Unchanged from round 3, stated in the code, and covered by no test because nothing here can restart a daemon mid-launch.

An issue pod's ephemeral claim is always `<pod>-issue`, so a replacement pod created before its predecessor's claim is reaped stays Pending until it is — about a second, measured, against a 120 s boot timeout.
